newsitem.title: UK: IRA claim Belfast rocket, leave six more bombs.
newsitem.headline: IRA claim Belfast rocket, leave six more bombs.

text.p: Irish republican guerrillas, fighting for an end to British rule in Northern Ireland, fired a rocket at law courts in Belfast on Monday, slightly injuring two people, and claimed to have planted bombs elsewhere in the city.
The action by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) raised the prospect of retaliation by pro-British Loyalist fighters.
Some reports said the rocket was fired from a passing car in a busy central shopping area.

It struck a police security checkpoint outside the court buildings, which are seen by the IRA as a symbol of British repression and have been frequently attacked by IRA guerrillas in their 28-year-old campaign.
A policeman suffered injuries to the ear and a woman inside the court building was blown off her feet by the blast. There were no serious casualties, police said.
A caller to a Belfast radio station, claiming IRA responsibility for the rocket attack, said the guerrillas had also left bombs at four hotels, at the city's main rail station and a bus station.
Sources at Downtown Radio station said the call with a recognised IRA identity codeword was made by someone speaking for the IRA's "Belfast Brigade".
Police said an initial search of the bomb locations pinpointed by the IRA had drawn a blank so far.
The president of the IRA's Sinn fein political wing, Gerry Adams, said the IRA attack was a "regrettable".
John Hunter, a lawyer in court at the time of the rocket attack, said: "I heard a bomb go off, there was momentary shock. We all realised it was a bomb."
The guerrillas are known to possess rocket-propelled grenades, bazookas and rocket launchers in a vast arsenal assembled on the international black market over two decades.
A car used in the attack was later found abandoned and ablaze in a Catholic section of Belfast -- a guerrilla tactic used to destroy any forensic evidence.

The IRA's ideological enemies, Protestant Loyalists who want Northern Ireland to remain British, said at the weekend they would end a two-year truce and go back to war if the IRA continued its guerrilla campaign.

Loyalists, so-called because of their allegiance to Britain, called a truce in October 1994 to win a seat for their political representatives at multiparty peace talks in Belfast. But they say their truce is under severe pressure because of IRA violence.
The IRA bombed British army headquarters in the province last October, killing one soldier and injuring 30. But recent attacks have been botched or foiled by security forces.
On New Year's Eve the guerrillas said they had abandoned a van carying a landmine in the grounds of Belfast castle. Tight security prevented them reaching their target.
The IRA has habitually attacked members of the 12,000-strong Royal Ulster Constabulary and Britain's 18,000 troops in the province during a quarter of a century of guerrilla war.
It ended a 17-month ceasefire last February and is demanding admission of its political arm, Sinn Fein, to the Belfast peace talks without preconditions.
Britain and the Irish Republic, co-sponsors of the talks, say Sinn Fein can only take part when the IRA has called a permanent end to its guerrilla war.
